sources: Health Practitioner Regulation National Law s.133
AHPRA Guidelines for advertising a regulated health service
TGA Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code / advertising health services FAQ
_meta.note: Term matches are INDICATORS requiring human review, not determinations of breach. AHPRA enforcement is risk-based and context matters.

tga_s4_branded.why: Schedule 4 prescription-only medicines cannot be advertised to the public in Australia. Naming a brand is the clearest form of breach and is what the TGA's Operation Redress audit counted. 'Botox' appeared 2,983 times across the 98 non-compliant sites it found.

tga_s4_generic.why: The TGA treats generic substance names and active ingredients the same as brand names. Acronyms, nicknames and hashtags count too if a consumer would read them as referring to the substance.

tga_s4_slang.why: The TGA explicitly names slang, abbreviations and hashtags as breaches. Operation Redress counted 435 uses of Botox slang variants alone.

tga_service_descriptors.why: The TGA previously permitted indirect descriptors like 'wrinkle reducing injections' when promoting a service. That position has tightened. 'Dermal filler' was the single most-counted flagged term in Operation Redress at 31,874 uses. Treat these as likely-problematic rather than certain.

ahpra_testimonial.why: s.133(1)(c) prohibits using testimonials about clinical aspects of a regulated health service in advertising. This is the single most common failure, and the one generalist marketers walk clients into because review widgets are their default playbook. Unsolicited reviews on third-party sites the practitioner does not control are treated differently — the breach is USING them in advertising.

ahpra_review_widgets.why: An embedded review widget on a regulated health service site republishes testimonials as advertising. Detected from raw HTML rather than visible text because the vendor name appears in script/iframe sources.

ahpra_before_after.why: Before/after imagery is heavily restricted — it must be genuine, comparable (same lighting/angle/preparation), carry appropriate disclaimers, and not create unreasonable expectation. Cosmetic procedures carry additional requirements post-2023.

ahpra_unreasonable_expectation.why: s.133(1)(d) prohibits advertising that creates an unreasonable expectation of beneficial treatment. Superlatives and absolute outcome claims are the usual trigger. Context matters heavily — 'best' in 'best practice' is fine, so review matches rather than counting them.

ahpra_inducement.why: s.133(1)(b) prohibits offering a gift, discount or inducement WITHOUT clearly stating the terms and conditions. The offer itself is not the breach — the missing terms are. These matches always need a human to check whether terms are present and visible.

ahpra_title_protection.why: Protected titles and specialist registration were tightened after the 2023 cosmetic surgery reforms. 'Cosmetic surgeon' in particular is now restricted, and US-style credential language misleads Australian consumers.

agency_compliance_claims.why: When auditing a competitor AGENCY rather than a clinic, these phrases mark the positioning they are claiming. Every specialist in this market claims compliance, so the claim itself is not a differentiator — it is the thing to test against their client work.
